    <item>
        <title>[$] Python's experimental JIT to be removed</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102102/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102102/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>Python's <a
href="https://docs.python.org/3.13/whatsnew/3.13.html#an-experimental-just-in-time-jit-compiler">experimental
just-in-time (JIT) compiler</a>, which was added to CPython in 2024 for the <a
href="https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3130/">3.13&#160;release</a>,
is on its way out. In June, the Python steering council <a
href="https://discuss.python.org/t/an-announcement-from-the-steering-council-regarding-the-jit-project/107638">announced</a>
that it was pausing work on the JIT in CPython's main branch until there was an
accepted <a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0001">Python Enhancement
Proposal</a> (PEP) that addressed concerns about maintenance, compatibility, and
set clear success metrics as well as a timeline for completion. After creating
<a href="https://peps.python.org/pep-0836/">PEP&#160;836</a> ("JIT Go Brrr: The
Path to a Supported JIT Compiler for CPython")
to try to meet the council's request, and after months of discussion, the
JIT maintainers have withdrawn the PEP. For now, it appears that development on
the once-promising project has come to an end.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:45:58 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] The first part of the 7.4 merge window</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1101211/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1101211/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Since the merge window for 7.4 opened, there have been 6,753 non-merge
changesets pulled into the mainline repository. Many more are expected,
especially given the possibility that this merge window will be extended to
three weeks. Still, even this initial set brought in a number of new features,
in addition to the continued general cleanups and security fixes that the kernel
has seen recently.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Fri, 23 Oct 2026 18:54:33 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Seeking smaller kernel stacks</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100271/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100271/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>Memory has always been a scarce resource in computing systems, but the
problem seems to have worsened recently.  In particular, the worldwide
shortage of memory chips has led to a renewed focus by systems developers
on reducing memory usage.  During the memory-management microconference at
the 2026 <a href="https://lpc.events/">Linux Plumbers Conference</a>, Will
Deacon discussed one specific consumer of memory that is being
re-examined: kernel stacks.
</description>
        <pubDate>Fri, 23 Oct 2026 14:59:24 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] The end of __get_user() and __put_user()</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102061/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1102061/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>Linus Torvalds rarely writes significant amounts of kernel code these days, so
the <a
href="https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git/commit/?id=22a78a25438d">merging</a>
of a 48-part patch series from him is an unusual event.  This series,
destined for the 7.4 kernel release, performs some long-delayed kernel
cleanup by removing a couple of the primitives used to access user-space memory
from the kernel.  What was once a best practice has long been superseded,
but it can take time for such changes to work their way through a body of
code this large.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 16:25:50 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Rust features in the future</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099606/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099606/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
There are several Rust features that kernel developers have been hoping to
stabilize, but Josh Triplett wanted to describe all of the <em>other</em>
features that the Rust project is currently working on. He spoke about the topic
at Kangrejos 2026, leaving the assembled kernel developers with several ideas
about how to use these upcoming Rust features in the kernel.
The features included refinements to the type system, small syntax improvements, and a
smarter borrow checker.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:19:56 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

        <item>
        <title>[$] Hash-based module integrity for reproducible distributions</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100026/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100026/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
        <description>We last looked in on <a href="https://lwn.net/Articles/1012946/">hash-based integrity
checking for kernel modules</a> just over a year and half ago.  Since that time,
the <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20260505-module-hashes-v5-0-e174a5a49fce@weissschuh.net/">patch
set</a> has undergone multiple revisions.  At the 2026 <a href="https://lpc.events/">Linux Plumbers Conference</a>
(LPC),  Thomas Weißschuh described the need for kernel-module integrity
guarantees while still providing reproducible builds, how his patches implement that, and some ideas for possible
further work.
</description>
        <pubDate>Wed, 21 Oct 2026 16:14:55 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Understanding Nix flakes</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094226/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1094226/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p><a href="https://wiki.nixos.org/wiki/Flakes">Nix flakes</a> are an
experimental feature of the <a
href="https://wiki.nixos.org/wiki/Nix_(package_manager)">Nix package-management
tool</a> designed to build projects in a more self-contained and reproducible
way. Despite the feature's experimental status, it has become increasingly
popular for open-source projects to publish <tt>flake.nix</tt> files that offer
predefined development environments and build automation even when those
repositories may not offer an upstream package or module for the <a
href="https://wiki.nixos.org/wiki/NixOS">NixOS Linux distribution</a>. Although
Nix flakes have a complicated history, and the path for stabilization is
uncertain, flakes can provide useful capabilities for projects that choose to
include them.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Wed, 21 Oct 2026 14:33:54 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] SUSE's efforts to disable setuid system-wide</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100257/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100257/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p>Setuid (and setgid) binaries have long been a source of headaches, and security
vulnerabilities, on Linux systems. They are largely seen as something to be
avoided; SUSE's security team, for example, <a
href="https://en.opensuse.org/openSUSE:Package_security_guidelines#Setuid_Binaries">forbids
the inclusion of setuid or setgid binaries in packages</a> unless they have been
reviewed and explicitly allowed. Thorsten Kukuk wants to go a step further and
disallow them entirely. At the <a
href="https://all-systems-go.io/">2026&#160;All&#160;Systems&#160;Go!</a> conference, he spoke
about his work to disable setuid system-wide, as well as some of the hurdles
that remain.</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Tue, 20 Oct 2026 18:36:10 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Discussing a rewrite of XArray</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100520/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100520/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
The work to support block sizes larger than the page size on XFS has been
difficult. Many users of XFS run stable kernels, which means that they aren't testing
new XFS code as it is released. That has made Daniel Gomez wonder whether
adopting Rust for some of the data structures underlying XFS, particularly
<a href="https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/xarray.html">
XArrays</a>, could reduce the number of bugs lurking in the code. At
Kangrejos 2026, he led a discussion about the potential problems with converting
XArray to Rust. The assembled kernel developers had a number of reasons to be
cautious about replacing the XArray code, but Gomez was determined to experiment
with the possibility, citing both security and performance improvements.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Tue, 20 Oct 2026 15:46:37 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Development statistics for the 7.3 kernel</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100241/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1100241/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>Linus Torvalds <a
href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/CAHk-=wgwnBm2zDdRM7u016NVHkv9KqbZW7AZ=8wZrqGyv_V+5A@mail.gmail.com/">released</a>
the 7.3 kernel, at the end of the usual nine-week development cycle, on
October&#160;18.  This cycle, abundantly fueled by LLM-assisted
contributions, broke just about every record imaginable.  As usual, we have
compiled some statistics showing how this release, which is expected to be
the next long-term-support (LTS) kernel, came together.  Also included is
an attempt to determine whether automated patch review is actually reducing
the number of bugs introduced into the kernel.
</description>
        <pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 15:45:24 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Cross-crate forward declarations in Rust</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099596/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099596/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Rust has several ad-hoc mechanisms to allow user code to influence how the
standard library executes. For example, custom panic handlers and custom
allocators both involve registering functions that core standard library code
needs to call. With more similar features planned,
Jana Dönszelmann spotted the developing pattern and put together a
general solution, introducing a safer, checked analogue of C's weak symbol
linking. At Kangrejos 2026, she explained how this new language feature works,
and proposed using it to clean up the kernel's handling of integer overflows in
Rust code.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Mon, 19 Oct 2026 13:50:49 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Safe self-referential data structures in kernel Rust</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099224/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099224/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Self-referential structures that can be used without unsafe code
have posed a problem for Rust for years.
There are many cases where a self-referential data structure is the elegant
algorithmic choice, but implementing it in accordance with Rust's lifetime rules
is all but impossible. At Kangrejos 2026, Gary Guo presented a clever solution
to the problem in the context of the kernel's
<a href="https://rust.docs.kernel.org/pin_init/index.html">
pin_init crate</a>, which helps with the creation of immovable data structures,
typically for interoperability with C. Guo's changes could help remove most of
the unsafe code related to lifetimes in the
<a href="https://rust-for-linux.com/nova-gpu-driver">
Nova driver</a> and, eventually, other Rust components.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 18:30:00 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Recent and future changes to the Linux NFS server</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098611/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098611/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>The NFS network filesystem protocol has a long history on Unix-like
operating systems (and beyond).  NFS is still evolving, though, and
implementations need to keep up.  At the 2026 <a
href="https://lpc.events/">Linux Plumbers Conference</a>, NFS developer
Jeff Layton gave an overview of recent enhancements to the Linux
implementation, along with some hints for what will be coming in the near
future.
</description>
        <pubDate>Fri, 16 Oct 2026 14:26:57 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>[$] Vendor hooks in the Android kernel</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098493/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098493/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>Since Android's inception, the kernels it has used have diverged
significantly from the mainline.  While many of those differences have been
resolved over time, and the move to the <a
href="https://source.android.com/docs/core/architecture/kernel/generic-kernel-image">generic
kernel image</a> has helped to bring Android closer, current devices still
carry a lot of out-of-tree changes.  The preferred form for such changes is
by way of <a
href="https://source.android.com/docs/core/architecture/kernel/kernel-code#vendor-hooks">vendor
hooks</a>.  At the <a href="https://lpc.events/event/20/">2026 Linux
Plumbers Conference</a>, Todd Kjos ran a fast-paced session in the Android
track to discuss vendor hooks and how they are used.
</description>
        <pubDate>Thu, 15 Oct 2026 15:09:15 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>

        <item>
        <title>Collaborating with out-of-tree tracers</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099300/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099300/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jake</dc:creator>
        <description><a href="https://lttng.org/">LTTng</a> creator Mathieu Desnoyers seems a
bit trapped in something of a <a
href="https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/catch-22">catch-22</a>.
At the 2026 <a href="https://lpc.events/">Linux Plumbers Conference</a>
(LPC), he led a discussion on the problem he is having in trying to
collaborate with other tracing projects (e.g. <a
href="https://docs.kernel.org/trace/ftrace.html">ftrace</a>, <a
href="https://perfwiki.github.io/main/">perf</a>) in the kernel.  The
feedback he has gotten, both over the years and more recently, does not
show a path that would allow him to contribute the 21-year-old
GPLv2-licensed LTTng tracing framework, or, incrementally, features from
it, to the mainline kernel.
</description>
        <pubDate>Wed, 14 Oct 2026 13:56:50 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>GCC development with large-language models</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098672/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1098672/</guid>
        <dc:creator>corbet</dc:creator>
        <description>After much deliberation, the GCC project recently came up with <a
href="https://gcc.gnu.org/ai-policy.html">a policy on the use of large
language models</a> for development of the compiler suite.  It is somewhat
restrictive, but still leaves room for LLMs in the development process.  At
the 2026 <a href="https://gnu-tools-cauldron.org/">GNU Tools Cauldron</a>,
Jeff Law and Kyrill Tkachov discussed how these tools have been useful for
them.
</description>
        <pubDate>Wed, 14 Oct 2026 13:13:53 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>KDE Linux at two</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099486/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099486/</guid>
        <dc:creator>jzb</dc:creator>
        <description><p><a href="https://linux.kde.org/">KDE&#160;Linux</a>, the KDE Project's second
stab at creating its own distribution, was first introduced as "Project Banana"
at the <a href="https://akademy.kde.org/2024/">Akademy conference in 2024</a> by
Harald Sitter. Nate Graham <a
href="https://pointieststick.com/2025/09/06/announcing-the-alpha-release-of-kde-linux/">announced</a>
the first alpha-quality release during <a
href="https://akademy.kde.org/2025/">Akademy&#160;2025</a>. Graham and Sitter
paired up at <a href="https://akademy.kde.org/2026/">Akademy&#160;2026</a> to 
provide an update on its progress, lay out plans for refining the distribution to
address user feedback, and discuss some of the problems that still need to be
dealt with. KDE Linux is still not-quite-ready for prime time, but Graham hopes
that it will be suitable for widespread use soon&mdash;for an undefined value of
"soon".</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 17:21:14 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
        <item>
        <title>Owning C types from Rust code</title>
        <link>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099015/</link>
        <guid>https://lwn.net/Articles/1099015/</guid>
        <dc:creator>daroc</dc:creator>
        <description><p>
Rust's system of ownership and borrowed references is convenient when it can
correctly model a program's needs. The
<a href="https://rust-for-linux.com/">
Rust for Linux project</a> has worked to
provide adapters between Rust's semantics and the existing C code
in the kernel. At Kangrejos 2026, Andreas Hindborg spoke about a
<a href="https://lwn.net/ml/all/20260910-unique-ref-v21-0-e83257373062@kernel.org/">
patch
series</a> implementing the next such adaptor: an <tt>Ownable</tt> trait for
representing objects that are allocated in C code, but which Rust code is responsible
for cleaning up (if not necessarily deallocating) when it is done with them.
He hoped to finally reach a consensus on the patch series, after months of
discussion on the mailing list.
</p>
</description>
        <pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 13:33:13 +0000</pubDate>
        </item>
